pages.text: Rain drummed on the roof of the bus. Swish, swish went the big wipers. Amin had the best seat on the bus: the window seat. Dad stood right beside him, holding the pole.

pages.text: Amin looked at his sun on the window. It was a very good sun. Then he looked at the old woman’s hand on the pole. It was shaking a little. What would you do?

pages.text: The old woman sat down with a long, happy “Aaah.” “Thank you,” she said. “Come and stand by me.” Dad put her bags down by her feet, and winked at Amin.

pages.text: The old woman looked at the window. “Is this your sun?” she asked. Amin nodded. “Then it needs a sea,” she said. With one finger, she drew little waves under the sun.

pages.text: “When I was a little girl,” she said, “I lived by the sea. Every morning I ran down to the waves.” Swish, swish went the wipers.

pages.text: She told Amin about white boats and warm sand. She told him about seagulls that cried over the waves. Amin drew a seagull on the window. It had very long wings. The old woman laughed.

pages.text: At her stop, the old woman picked up her bags. “Goodbye, little painter,” she said, and waved. Amin waved back. On the steamy window, his sun still shone over her little sea.

activity.title: Hopscotch from Long Ago
activity.goal: Learn a game from an older person by listening to their rules and playing it their way.

steps.caption: Ask an older person: how did you play?
Throw the sock. Hop their way.

activity.safety: Play on a flat, dry place away from cars, with a grown-up watching. Chalk is for the ground, not for the mouth. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Amin greets an old woman and gives her his seat, and she shares her memories with him. This activity is another way of showing respect to older people: asking them to teach us something, and doing it their way. Ask a grandparent or an older neighbour how they played hopscotch as a child. Many families in Israel and in Denmark know a version, and the squares and rules differ a lot. Help the child ask: “How did you play? What did the squares look like?” The older person describes or draws the grid, and the child copies it with chalk. A rolled-up sock makes a good marker: it does not roll away or bounce. Then play by their rules, even if they seem strange. If the older person cannot hop, they can be the judge or keep count. Fifteen to twenty minutes is plenty. To make it easier, draw a short grid of four squares. To make it harder, ask a second older person and compare the two games.
activity.inClass: Invite a grandparent to the class to teach their hopscotch. Before the visit, the children prepare two or three questions and practise greeting the guest. Groups of four or five each draw the guest’s grid in the yard and play by the guest’s rules, while the guest visits each group. At the end, the children thank the guest.
